title: TheHive
subtitle: Case management / SOAR — where a Wazuh alert becomes a tracked investigation.

intro.text: Wazuh detects and correlates; it has no concept of a "case," an assigned analyst, or a task checklist. TheHive is the layer above that — every alert at level 7 or higher gets pushed into it automatically, where it can be triaged, promoted to a case using a standardized template, and worked through task by task.

It runs on its own dedicated VM (thehive-vm, 8GB RAM / 4 vCPU / 80GB, bridged onto the same LAN as every other agent), as a Docker Compose stack: TheHive 5.2, Cortex 3.1.8, Cassandra 4.1 for storage, and Elasticsearch 7.17.13 as the shared search index.

blocks.text: Four services, one docker-compose.yml. Cassandra and Elasticsearch come up first, then Cortex, then TheHive last — TheHive needs a working Cortex API key already available in its config before it starts up usefully.

blocks.code:
services:
  cassandra:
    image: cassandra:4.1
    environment:
      - MAX_HEAP_SIZE=1G
      - HEAP_NEWSIZE=1G
      - CASSANDRA_CLUSTER_NAME=thp

  elasticsearch:
    image: docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch:7.17.13
    environment:
      - discovery.type=single-node
      - xpack.security.enabled=false
      - "ES_JAVA_OPTS=-Xms1g -Xmx1g"

  cortex:
    image: thehiveproject/cortex:3.1.8
    depends_on: [elasticsearch]
    ports: ["9001:9001"]
    volumes:
      - ./cortex/application.conf:/etc/cortex/application.conf
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock

  thehive:
    image: strangebee/thehive:5.2
    depends_on: [cassandra, elasticsearch, cortex]
    ports: ["9000:9000"]
    volumes:
      - ./thehive/application.conf:/etc/thehive/application.conf

blocks.title: One host-level gotcha before any of this works
blocks.text: Elasticsearch requires the kernel setting `vm.max_map_count >= 262144` on the actual VM host, set via /etc/sysctl.d/ before the containers can start — a container-level fix alone isn't enough.
On first boot, TheHive imports 707 MITRE ATT&CK patterns automatically — the same taxonomy already used throughout the Wazuh alerts and case templates on this site.

sections.title: Organizations and users — the lesson that mattered most

blocks.title: The default organization is a trap
blocks.text: Both TheHive and Cortex ship with a reserved default organization ("admin" in TheHive, "cortex" in Cortex) meant purely for platform administration — creating other organizations and users. It is not where real work happens, and it deliberately can't do real work: a user in that org can't hold the roles needed to create alerts, enable analyzers, or manage cases. The first real API call against it failed with a blunt `403 — you don't have the permission manageAlert/create`, which is exactly the platform's intended behavior, not a bug.

The fix is the same in both tools: create a second, real working organization (this lab uses `soc-lab` in both TheHive and Cortex), and inside it create two kinds of accounts — a normal, password-based analyst account for humans, and a Service-type account authenticating only via API key for automation.
TheHive: creating the working org

items: Log in as the initial admin@thehive.local superadmin account (Organisations → the reserved admin org).
Organisations → + → create a new organisation, e.g. soc-lab.
Inside soc-lab → Users → Add User → a normal account with the org-admin profile, a real password, used for day-to-day investigation.
A second Service-type user (e.g. wazuh-integration@soc-lab.local) with the analyst profile, no password — only an API key — used exclusively by the Wazuh integration script.

blocks.text: Cortex: the exact same pattern, different terminology

Cortex uses granular role checkboxes instead of a single profile dropdown: read, analyze, orgAdmin. A working-org user needs all three to browse and enable analyzers from the catalog — the reserved default org's role selector only ever offers "superadmin", which is itself the tell that you're in the wrong org.

Rather than starting every investigation from a blank case, four templates were created via the API (a short Python script using only the standard library's urllib, no external dependencies) so any alert can be promoted straight into a structured checklist.

rows: 6 — confirm source/dest, map to MITRE T1046/T1595.002, verify authorized machine, decide close or escalate
7 — count attempts, map to T1110.001/003, check for a successful login after failures, force reset if compromised
8 — identify affected files, T1486/T1490, isolate host, preserve evidence, identify patient zero, restore from backup
7 — deliberately mirrors the exact fix/mitigate/accept workflow used for the 24 real CVEs on the CVE Management page

blocks.text: The CVE template's last task is literally "create/update the file in the vulnerabilidades/ repository folder" — the case-management workflow and the actual documentation habit are the same process, not two separate things.

Wazuh has no built-in TheHive connector. The bridge uses Wazuh's own custom-integration mechanism (wazuh-integratord), which calls a script on every alert matching a configured level, passing the alert file path plus an API key and hook URL as arguments.

The script itself (a wrapper shell script plus a Python file, the standard pattern for all custom Wazuh integrations) reads the alert JSON, maps the Wazuh rule.level to a TheHive severity (1–4), and POSTs to TheHive's alert-creation API with a Bearer token.
Two real bugs on the way to a working integration

items: The terminal's line editor was silently corrupting large pasted heredocs containing curly braces (common in Python f-strings). Worked around by base64-encoding the whole script locally and decoding it in a single line on the remote host — completely immune to shell/editor character interpretation.

The first live test returned HTTP 403 with the same manageAlert/create permission error described above — using the reserved admin organization's API key instead of a working-org key. Switching to a soc-lab-scoped API key fixed it immediately.

blocks.title: Validation
blocks.text: A manual test alert returned HTTP 201 — and within minutes, real Wazuh alerts (a "Listened ports status changed" event and a rootcheck anomaly) appeared in TheHive's queue with zero further manual action, confirming the integratord daemon was calling the script correctly in production, not just in the manual test.

sections.title: Reading a real alert end to end — worked example

blocks.text: A genuine alert that arrived automatically through the integration above, exactly as it appears in TheHive's General tab — not a constructed example. This is the same 5-question triage flow used on the Wazuh page, walked through on a live case.

blocks.code:
{
  "timestamp": "2026-08-05T07:13:50.366+0200",
  "rule": {
    "level": 7,
    "description": "Integrity checksum changed.",
    "id": "550",
    "mitre": { "id": ["T1565.001"], "tactic": ["Impact"], "technique": ["Stored Data Manipulation"] },
    "firedtimes": 24,
    "groups": ["ossec", "syscheck", "syscheck_entry_modified", "syscheck_file"]
  },
  "agent": { "id": "005", "name": "tales-desktop", "ip": "192.168.178.92" },
  "manager": { "name": "soc-server" },
  "full_log": "File '/etc/cups/subscriptions.conf.O' modified\nMode: realtime\nChanged attributes: size,inode,mtime,md5,sha1,sha256\nSize changed from '397' to '699'\nOld md5sum was: '6ae849634dec4fa5803ae7d8d23fa4da'\nNew md5sum is : 'c78975ea11f60fee3c7252e019985309'",
  "syscheck": {
    "path": "/etc/cups/subscriptions.conf.O",
    "mode": "realtime",
    "uid_after": "0",
    "gid_after": "7",
    "uname_after": "root",
    "gname_after": "lp",
    "changed_attributes": ["size", "inode", "mtime", "md5", "sha1", "sha256"],
    "event": "modified"
  },
  "decoder": { "name": "syscheck_integrity_changed" },
  "location": "syscheck"
}

blocks.text: 1 — Recognize

rule.id 550, level 7 — a generic Wazuh FIM "content modified" alert, not the lab's own critical rule 100200 (level 12, scoped to /srv/media). The rule.mitre.id T1565.001 ("Stored Data Manipulation") is Wazuh's default, generic mapping for any file content change — it categorizes the technique, it does not by itself mean anything malicious happened.
2 — Contextualize

syscheck.path is /etc/cups/subscriptions.conf.O — CUPS, the Linux printing subsystem, rewriting its own subscription state file. Ownership after the change: uname_after root, gname_after lp ("line printer" group) — exactly consistent with the printing service editing its own configuration. Critically, this path is not under /srv/media (the protected asset) and not a security-sensitive file like /etc/passwd or /etc/sudoers.
3 — Correlate

rule.firedtimes: 24 — this exact rule has already fired 24 times for this kind of event on this agent. A high firedtimes count on a low-severity rule is itself a correlation signal: it points to a recurring, established background pattern rather than a one-off, novel event worth escalating.
4 — Decide
Everything points the same direction — file path, ownership, recurrence — so the reasonable call is: expected system behavior, not a security event. Close it, don't promote it to a case.
5 — Document and resolve
Two concrete actions in TheHive, depending on what the alert turns out to be:

items: If it's confirmed benign (this case): close the alert directly from the alert list — no case needed. Since this exact pattern already has firedtimes: 24, it's a strong candidate for a tuning rule back on Wazuh, the same pattern already used for rule 100101 (which downgrades Suricata's "Ethertype unknown" noise): add a local_rules.xml rule that lowers the severity of syscheck changes specifically under /etc/cups/, so this stops reaching TheHive's queue at all while paths that actually matter stay untouched.

If instead the context pointed the other way — an unfamiliar path, unexpected ownership, no prior firedtimes history — the same alert would be promoted straight into a case using the Ransomware / FIM Critical Alert template from the section above, and worked through its 8-task checklist.

blocks.title: The other tabs on an alert
blocks.text: Observables, TTPs, Similar Cases and Similar Alerts exist for exactly this kind of decision: Similar Alerts would show every prior firedtimes:24 occurrence at a glance, without needing to go back to Wazuh's own Discover screen to reconstruct the history manually.
